Surah al-Fatihah (The Opening) is Meccan. It has seven verses, counting the basmalah (the phrase "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"), if it is part of it; in that case the seventh verse is "The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour" to the end. If the basmalah is not part of it, the seventh verse is "other than those who have earned anger" to the end. And the word "qulu" (say) is to be understood at its beginning, so that what precedes "You alone we worship" fits it, since the surah is then part of what the servants say.

The Commentary of al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti (Tafsir al-Jalalayn) on surah 1, verse 2:

﴿Al-hamdu lillah﴾ (All praise is for Allah) is a declarative sentence (jumla khabariyya), by whose content is intended praise of Allah, on the basis that He is the owner of all praise from creation, or the one deserving that they praise Him. And Allah is a proper name (ʿalam) for the one worshipped in truth.

﴿Rabb al-ʿalamin﴾ (Lord of the worlds): that is, the owner of all creation, of humankind, jinn, angels, animals and others. Each of these is called an ʿalam (world); one says ʿalam al-insan (the world of humankind), ʿalam al-jinn (the world of the jinn), and so on. The masculine plural with the suffix -ina and -un (ya' and nun) was predominantly applied to those endowed with reason (ulu al-ʿilm) over others. The word ʿalam is derived from ʿalama (sign, mark), because it is a sign pointing to its Creator (mujidihi).

Commentary of al-Mahalli and al-Suyuti (Tafsir al-Jalalayn) on surah 1, verse 3:

﴿The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾. That is, Possessor of mercy, which is the will of good for its people.

Commentary of al-Mahalli & al-Suyuti (Tafsir al-Jalalayn) on surah 1, verse 4:

﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ i.e., the recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection. It is singled out for mention because no one has apparent sovereignty on that day except Allah the Exalted, as evidenced by ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today? To Allah﴾. As for the one who reads "Mālik" (Malik), its meaning is "the Owner of all the affair on the Day of Resurrection," or He is continually described by that, like "the Forgiver of sin" (ghāfir al-dhanb), so its occurrence as an adjective of a definite noun is correct.

Commentary of al-Mahalli & al-Suyuti (Tafsir al-Jalalayn) on surah 1, verse 5:

﴿Thee alone do we worship, and Thee alone do we ask for help﴾ — meaning: we single You out for worship, whether of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) or other acts, and we seek help for the worship and for other matters.

Tafsir al-Jalalayn on surah 1, verse 6:

﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾. That is, direct us to it. And it (﴿الصِّراط المُسْتَقِيم﴾, "the straight path") is substituted for (﴿اهْدِنا﴾'s object)... 

Translation:

﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, that is, direct us to it. And it (the straight path) is a substitute (badal) for it (the preceding object).

"The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor" — with guidance — (this is) a substitution (badal) from "those," because of its connection to it. "Not of those who have evoked (Your) anger" — and they are the Jews — "nor" — and not — "of those who are astray" — and they are the Christians. The point of the substitution is to convey that the guided are neither Jews nor Christians. And Allah knows best what is correct, and to Him is the return and the final resort. And may Allah send abundant blessings and peace upon our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and upon his family and companions.
